title: Lists and indexing
goals: Distinguish a list index from the value stored at that position
Read and update an item using a valid index
Trace a loop through list values and test an empty list

prerequisite.prompt: What values does range(3) supply? How many iterations occur?
prerequisite.answer: 0, 1 and 2; three iterations. The stop value 3 is excluded.

vocabulary: An integer position used to access an item
The number of items in a collection
One value stored in a collection
An error raised when an index is outside a sequence

blocks.text: A fictional supply shelf has three trays with counts 4, 7 and 4 in that order. Store them as counts = [4, 7, 4]. Square brackets enclose the list and commas separate its items. The order matters: the first and third trays contain equal values but occupy different positions.

Python counts positions from zero. counts[0] reads the first item, counts[1] the second and counts[2] the third. len(counts) is 3 because there are three items. It is a count, not the last nonnegative index. This lesson uses integer counts and nonnegative indices; Python also supports negative indices, which are outside our current indexing convention.

lesson.title: Read a value and change one position

blocks.title: Positions and stored counts
blocks.caption: Equal stored values do not imply equal positions. There is no item at index 3.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
counts = [4, 7, 4]
print(len(counts))
print(counts[0])
print(counts[1])
counts[1] = 9
print(counts)

The printed lines are 3, 4, 7 and [4, 9, 4]. The assignment counts[1] = 9 replaces the item at index 1; it does not add a fourth item or change the two other values. The length stays 3. A recorded count can be changed by code without proving that the physical tray really contains that many objects.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
counts = [4, 7, 4]
total = 0
for count in counts:
    total = total + count
print(total)

This fresh script prints 15. for count in counts supplies the stored values, not the indices. Both copies of 4 are processed because both are items. For an empty list written [], the body runs zero times and total stays 0. For [7], it runs once and prints 7.

blocks.label: Change only the list to [2, 0, 5]. Trace the three additions and state the final output. Explain why the middle item is processed even though its value is zero.

blocks.text: This deliberately faulty script raises IndexError. The list has three items, but its nonnegative indices are 0, 1 and 2. Replace 3 with 2 to read the third item, which is 4. For any nonempty list, len(counts) - 1 identifies the last item using a nonnegative index. An empty list has no valid item index.

Avoid confusing values with positions: for count in counts followed by counts[count] would try indices 4, 7 and 4 in this example. If you need both, use for index in range(len(counts)) and read counts[index]. If you only need a total, looping directly through values is simpler.

Before running a script, sketch positions above the stored values. Test an empty list, a one-item list and a list with repeated values. These cases reveal different mistakes. A total alone loses order: [4, 7, 4] and [7, 4, 4] both total 15 even though their first items differ. Data checks should retain the detail needed for the question.

blocks.label: A learner uses counts[len(counts)] to read the final item. Explain the error for [8, 3] and give a valid nonnegative index. Explain why your repair still needs an empty-list check.

workbook.title: Separate index and value
workbook.prompt: For counts = [4, 7, 4], give the length, valid nonnegative indices and value at index 1. Explain how the two items with value 4 differ.
workbook.answer: Length 3; indices 0, 1, 2; counts[1] is 7. The equal values occupy different positions, indices 0 and 2.

workbook.title: Trace an update
workbook.prompt: Start with counts = [4, 7, 4]. Run counts[0] = 6. Write the resulting list, its length and the value at index 2. Predict before running.
workbook.answer: The result is [6, 7, 4]; length remains 3; index 2 still holds 4. Only the first item was replaced.

workbook.title: Repair a position mistake
workbook.prompt: A learner loops with for count in counts and tries to read counts[count] for counts = [4, 7, 4]. Identify the first attempted index and error. Explain how to print each value directly.
workbook.answer: The first count is 4, so counts[4] raises IndexError. The loop variable already holds each value. Use an indented print(count) to print 4, 7 and 4 on separate lines.

workbook.title: Process new data independently
workbook.prompt: Start with readings = [3, 0, 3, 2]. Replace the second item with 5 using its index. Write a loop that adds all updated readings and prints one final total. Trace every update of the total. Then test the summing part alone on [] and [6].
workbook.answer: Use readings[1] = 5, giving [3, 5, 3, 2]. Initialize total = 0 before for reading in readings, add reading inside, and print outside. Running totals are 3, 8, 11, 13; final 13. Summing [] gives 0 and [6] gives 6. The replacement line itself requires at least two items.

workbook.title: Keep the information you need
workbook.prompt: Compare [1, 5, 2] and [5, 1, 2]. State their totals and first items. Would storing only the total answer which first item was larger? Explain.
workbook.answer: Both total 8. Their first items are 1 and 5, so the second list has the larger first item. A total alone discards the order and cannot answer this question.

teacher.background: Teach lists as ordered collections, with index and value kept distinct. The first exercises use nonnegative indices, although Python also permits negative indexing. Reference: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html#lists. Do not imply that updating a record changes or verifies the physical object represented.
materials: Four position cards numbered 0 through 3 and movable value cards
Blank trace table and separate predicted and observed output columns
sessions: Retrieve range(3) and its excluded stop.
Place value cards under position cards and complete W1.
Run the worked read and update script, then complete W2.
Trace the value loop and answer the guided question.
Retrieve the distinction between length and final index.
Predict the faulty access before running; use W3 to repair value versus index confusion.
Collect W4 independently, keeping the replacement step separate from empty-list summation.
Discuss W5 and use the exit to diagnose indexing assumptions.
teacher.guidedAnswer: For [2, 0, 5], totals become 2, 2, 7. Output is 7. Zero is still an item and its iteration still executes. Exit: len([8, 3]) is 2, but index 2 is outside the list. Last nonnegative index is 1, whose value is 3. An empty list has no last item, so a length check is required before access.
misconceptions: Length is the last nonnegative index
Length counts items; the last nonnegative index of a nonempty list is one less.
A loop variable always contains an index
A direct list loop supplies stored values.
Updating one item grows the list
Assignment at an existing index replaces that item; length is unchanged.
Repeated values are processed only once
Each position contributes one item, even when values repeat.
teacher.assessment: W4 must use index 1 for the second item, retain all four items, produce the full trace and output 13, and obtain 0 and 6 when testing only summation. After support, retry [2, 2, 1], replace the first item with 4, and sum: updated list [4, 2, 1], totals 4, 6, 7. Then sum [] and [5] for outputs 0 and 5. Record support before judging independence.
teacher.support: Keep position cards fixed while moving value cards. Permit an oral trace and provide a blank grid. Extension: write a guarded final-item reader that prints Empty when len(readings) == 0, otherwise prints readings[len(readings) - 1]. Test [] and [6].
